title: two Error classes in one failure channel whose durable contract identities collide are rejected, not silently merged into one variant
notes: specification/failures.mdx:209 (Locked): 'Handler selection MUST use compiler-stable nominal identity, not a forgeable user _tag or minifier-sensitive constructor name in compiled artifacts.' Read across the durable boundary, an identity is the key a decoder on the far side selects a handler by, so stability without INJECTIVITY is worthless: two declared Error classes arriving under one identity is precisely a forgeable key, and a decoder handed one of them would run the other's handler. `an-actions-failure-channel-mints-one-identity-per-error-class` pins the benign half of that obligation (two classes, two identities). This case pins the hostile half, and it is the half a compiler can only satisfy by refusing. `$Failed` and `_Failed` are two distinct declarations whose durable CONTRACT identities normalize to one string; both backends must refuse the program rather than mint a colliding pair. WHAT THIS CASE PINS: the code, the authored position, and — new as of 2026-08-27 — the PAYLOAD, on both backends. Column 10 on line 20 is the `Pick.run(...)` call node. WHY THE MESSAGE IS PINNED NOW AND WAS DELIBERATELY NOT PINNED BEFORE: both backends used to answer SMITHERS4112, 'higher-order and dynamic calls are unavailable in durable source lowering', which is FALSE of this program — there is no higher-order call and no dynamic call in it; `Pick.run({ key: input.key })` is an ordinary compiler-bound Action call. The reference reached that sentence only by falling through to the generic tail of `lowerExpression` (poc/src/durable/source-compiler.ts), and the Go fork reproduced it verbatim to hold backend agreement, so the verdict was right and the stated reason was a swallow artifact in two places. Declaring `messageContains` against THAT sentence would have ratified the misdescription as the contract, which is why the earlier revision of this file pinned only the code and the position and said so. The collision now has its own diagnostic, SMITHERS4124, in both implementations, at the same node the old code reported: the reference carries the collision's structured reason out of `deriveSameFileActions`' catch in `collidingActionsBySymbol` and re-reports it at the authored `run` call, and the Go bridge's `durableFailureIdentityCollides` returns the colliding pair instead of a bool and reports it from `lowerAction`. With a purpose-built diagnostic the payload finally IS the promise, so `messageContains` is declared — and it names the smallest fragment that carries it, both class names, rather than the sentence around them. The identity string is deliberately NOT in the fragment: it embeds each backend's logical file name for the compiled unit, which is not the same string on both sides and is not what this case is about. WHY SMITHERS4124 AND NOT SMITHERS4114: the migration plan proposed 4114 as 'the natural neighbour', and that was wrong on both counts. 4114 is TAKEN in the reference, where it means 'Action id <id> resolves to incompatible durable contracts' at five call sites — a different rule about one id with two contracts, not two classes with one identity — and it does not exist in the Go bridge at all. 4100-4123 are all in use across the two backends and 4199 is the durable internal-error code, so 4124 is the next free code in the family. WHAT IS NOT A GAP: the same-NAME family (two classes both spelled `Failed`) is not filed as a case. Both backends refuse it, but at different codes — SMITHERS1150 on the fork, SMITHERS4100/4112 on the reference — which is a both-closed divergence in reasoning, not a fail-open, and pinning it would freeze two unrelated rules against each other. Nor is the collision reached through `fanOut` or `loopWhile` filed here: the reference reports SMITHERS4124 for those forms too, but the Go bridge does not implement `fanOut`/`loopWhile` at all and refuses them wholesale as outside its durable subset, so a case would pin a pre-existing subset divergence rather than this rule. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: mutating the declared line from 20 to 21 turns the case red on BOTH backends with the position diff printed; mutating the declared code from SMITHERS4124 back to SMITHERS4112 turns it red on BOTH backends; and mutating `messageContains` to the retired sentence 'higher-order and dynamic calls' turns it red on BOTH backends with the message diff printed — which is the assertion that the earlier revision of this file could not make. The file was restored byte-identically after every mutation (sha256 recorded in the lane report). The paired negative control is `two-error-classes-with-distinct-durable-identities-compile`, which holds the other direction: it must keep compiling and RUNNING on both backends, so a collision check that over-fires on any two error classes turns that case red instead of passing silently. Before the Go identity fix this case could not have been written: the fork's `actionFor` set the error schema from a legacy placeholder and never read an Action's declared failure channel at all, so it compiled and ran this program.
